independent_translation: On the shore there are three men and one ship. A certain man says: 'Who is the man who has that ship?' His companion says: 'The man is my companion. He has the fish that we see.' 'To whom do you give the fish?' 'I give it to the man who helped me.' 'Which ship does he have?' 'He has the little ship that you saw.'
reading_findings: The participant roles are coherent: one man asks his companion about the third man.
First fiscas is accusative plural; later fisc/hine is one fish from the set, which is a natural contextual restriction.
Męnn is dative singular after sęlle; se in the following relative is nominative singular as the subject of healp. Their differing cases are deliberate and intelligible.
Ðæt in ðæt ðe ðū gesāwe is neuter accusative singular, the object of gesāwe, and gesāwe is the second-person singular preterite.
No repair is requested on independent reading. Contract and learner explanations must explicitly establish questions, relative use of demonstratives, and sum before this text.

example_findings: Example 14 requires learners to retain dative ðǣm within the relative, because helpan governs the dative; the English whom cannot determine the Old English case.
Example 15 hulpe agrees with second-person ðū; sęle is singular imperative. This directly supports the agreement need of Cook I.8.17.
Example 7 ǣnigne fisc is formally singular ('any fish' or 'a fish at all'), not an Old English plural. Key alternatives should preserve that distinction.
Example 5 needs the two-person context already specified by its author; no extra context-dependent pronoun use is inferred from the isolated wording.

later_genitive_relative_example_check.public_text: Se mann, ðæs scip ic geseah, is gōd.
later_genitive_relative_example_check.independent_translation: The man whose ship I saw is good.
analysis: Se mann is nominative masculine singular, the subject of is; gōd is its strong nominative masculine singular predicate adjective.

Ðæs is a genitive masculine singular relative referring to mann. It agrees with that antecedent in gender and number, but its genitive case comes from its own role as the possessor-dependent of scip inside the relative clause.
Scip is accusative neuter singular, the direct object of geseah; ic is nominative singular and geseah is first-person singular preterite. The genitive relative is not the subject or object of saw.
The antecedent is nominative while the relative is genitive. The clause identifies the man through the ship I saw; it makes no causal claim that seeing his ship makes him good.
This illustrates the already selected ordinary genitive-relative function. It adds no lexical system or earlier-form milestone, and does not require an interrogative or free-choice use.

new_scope.construction: Ordinary relative genitive dependent inside its clause, with nominative antecedent outside.
